newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa prime likely to fall by end August-survey.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa prime likely to fall by end August-survey.

text.p: South Africa's prime interest rate would be cut by 25 basis points by the end of August, WorldGroup Banking said in its latest interest rate forecast.
Eight economists participating in the June survey forecast prime to drop to 20 percent from 20.25 percent currently.
Other rates forecast were also expected to decline over the next quarter.
The 90-day BA rate was seen declining to 15.25 percent while the most likely value for the 12 month NCD rate was estimated at 15.70 percent over the same period.
The BA rate is currently at between 15.45 to 15.60 percent, while 12 month NCD rates were last quoted at 15.95 percent offered.

On the fixed income market, the yield on the E168 stock was forecast to fall to 14.62 percent -- from its most recent level of 14.88 percent -- but could lose as much as 100 points off its current level.
In the half year scenario up to November 1997, rates were seen continuing their easier trend.
Prime was expected a full percent lower at 19.25 percent and the 90-day BA rate was seen at 14.45 percent by the end of November.
The most likely value for the 12 month NCD rate was 14.95 percent, a decline of 100 points from its latest trading level on Monday.
Economists said rates were expected to ease across the board in the longer term with prime between one and three percent easier and most likely at 18.50 percent.
Factors taken into account in formulating the forecast included concern over the effects of the relaxation in foreign exchange controls on July 1.
"Despite the record reserves (of 21.80 billion rand) reported (in May), South Africa remains a country with one of the shortest import covers," the survey said.
"This, coupled with the high level of short-term foreign debt should encourage caution prior to dropping rates," it added.
But the recent increase in reserves was encouraging and should take pressure off the balance of payments.
It said credit demand remained unacceptably high although demand for asset-based financing appeared to be slowing.
Inflation was still high but a decline was anticipated along with the economic slowdown, which appeared sharper than expected.
Year-on-year consumer inflation came in at 9.9 percent in April, nudged up from 9.6 percent in March mainly by increased medical costs.
